title: Butter and emulsions
intro: How butter, yolk, acid and water are coaxed into one smooth sauce, and why they part again. From beurre blanc to mayonnaise, the same physics holds every one of them together.

entries.title: Beurre blanc
entries.summary: White butter: a sharp reduction of white wine, vinegar and shallot with cold butter whisked in piece by piece over low heat. No egg yolks hold it, only the butter itself, so it lives in a narrow warm window.
entries.guest: Beurre blanc is a warm, silky butter sauce sharpened with white wine and shallot, a classic for fish. On our Redfish Véronique it carries preserved lemon, salty and perfumed.

paras: Beurre blanc means white butter. It is a warm sauce made by boiling white wine, white wine vinegar and finely chopped shallot down to a few sharp spoonfuls, called the reduction, then whisking in cold butter a few pieces at a time over low heat. Cooks call this mounting the butter. The butter does not simply melt: it becomes a pale, glossy sauce about as thick as single cream (light cream), tasting of butter and acid at once.

What matters is what is missing: no egg yolk, as in hollandaise, and no flour. Butter is roughly four parts fat to one part water and milk solids. Whisked cold into a hot reduction, it softens rather than melting outright, and its fat breaks into tiny droplets held apart in the water by the butter's own milk proteins. Keep those droplets apart and the sauce stays creamy; let them run together and it turns to oil.

Put the wine, vinegar and shallot in a small, heavy pan and boil it until only about 2 tbsp (30 ml) of syrupy liquid remains, five to eight minutes. If the house adds cream, it goes in now and is reduced by half. Turn the heat to its lowest. The butter should be cold from the fridge, cut into 2 cm cubes.

Whisk in two or three cubes. As they soften and the sauce turns creamy, add two more, whisking or swirling the pan all the while, and lift the pan off the heat whenever it feels hot to the hand. Keep going until all the butter is in, three to five minutes in all. Season with salt, white pepper and a little lemon, then strain out the shallot or leave it in for a rustic sauce.

Hold it warm, roughly 55 to 60°C (131 to 140°F), on the back of the stove or in a bain-marie, a pan set in warm water. Much hotter and the emulsion loosens and the butterfat oils out; let it cool towards body heat and the fat begins to set, so the sauce thickens, dulls and splits when it is warmed again. That window straddles the FDA Food Code's hot-holding line of 57°C (135°F), so kitchens make it in small batches and, under the Food Code's time rule, discard each within four hours, sooner if the chef's written schedule says so.

Lemon, lime or orange juice and zest make a citrus beurre blanc; chives, chervil or tarragon stirred in at the end make a herb version. Red wine and red wine vinegar in the reduction give beurre rouge, a rosy butter sauce often served with salmon or red meat.

Many restaurants add a spoonful of double cream (heavy cream), reduced by half, before the butter, to steady the sauce through a busy service. It is a restaurant habit: purists leave it out, and a cook follows the house.

A beurre blanc fails three ways: too hot, or the butter added too fast, and it oils out into a thin, greasy pool; too cool, and it sets thick, dull and grainy; under-reduced, and it is thin and weak, the butter and acid diluted by water. Rescuing a sauce that has fully split is taught with how emulsions break.

Tradition credits beurre blanc to Clémence Lefeuvre, who cooked river fish at her inn at La Chebuette, in Saint-Julien-de-Concelles on the Loire just upstream of Nantes; the dates differ from one account to the next. The favourite story says she set out to make a béarnaise for pike and forgot the yolks and the tarragon; some tellings set that slip in the kitchen of the Château de Goulaine, where she is said to have cooked for the Marquis de Goulaine. Either way it became the Loire's sauce for river fish.

At Brennan's it is a preserved lemon beurre blanc on the Redfish Véronique. Lemon cured in salt and its own juice for weeks gives the sauce a salty, perfumed edge rather than plain sourness, which suits a flaky fish.

Say burr BLAHN, with no K sound at the end, and describe it as a warm butter sauce with white wine and shallot, bright rather than heavy. Held only just warm, it leaves the pass, the counter where plates leave the kitchen, the moment the plate is up. Every allergen or diet question goes to the kitchen and the service note.

entries.title: Beurre monté
entries.summary: Butter whisked piece by piece into a little boiling water until it becomes a creamy, pourable liquid. Neutral, with no acid and no reduction, it is a cooking medium for poaching lobster and fish, glazing vegetables and keeping food moist.
entries.guest: Beurre monté is butter whisked with a little water so it stays creamy instead of oily. Lobster or fish gently poached in it stays tender and moist.

paras: Beurre monté means mounted butter, from monter au beurre, the kitchen phrase for whisking butter into a liquid. It is butter emulsified into a spoonful of boiling water until the whole pan becomes a smooth, creamy liquid that pours like single cream (light cream). It tastes of nothing but sweet butter, and that is the point: it is less a sauce than a cooking medium, a warm butter bath.

Butter is already an emulsion, about four fifths fat with a little water and milk protein worked through it. Whisked into a little water a few pieces at a time, its fat breaks into tiny droplets held apart by the butter's own milk proteins, so the liquid stays creamy. Melt the same butter on its own and it separates: clear fat floating on a milky layer.

Bring about 2 tbsp (30 ml) of water to the boil in a small, heavy pan, then turn the heat down to low. Whisk in cold butter in 2 cm cubes, two or three at a time, adding more as each lot turns creamy. Once the emulsion has taken, after the first 100 g or so, the butter can go in faster. Keep whisking until it is all in. A large batch for poaching is built exactly the same way, from a little water up.

Hold it at roughly 70 to 85°C (158 to 185°F). In that window it stays creamy and pourable and will sit happily on the station. Past about 88°C (190°F), and certainly at a boil, the emulsion breaks into fat and water. A thermometer in the pan is worth more than a guess.

Cooks reach for it in four ways. Lobster, shrimp or delicate fish are poached in it slowly, so the flesh cooks gently and stays tender and moist. Cooked meat and fish waiting at the pass, the counter where plates leave the kitchen, are dipped or brushed with it so they keep their sheen and do not dry out. Carrots, turnips or peas are tossed in it to glaze them. And a spoonful finishes a sauce, adding body and gloss; that finishing technique is taught under monter au beurre.

Beurre blanc is its close cousin, built the same way. The difference is the base. Beurre blanc mounts butter into a sharp reduction of wine, vinegar and shallot and is served as a sauce in its own right. Beurre monté uses plain water, with no reduction and no acid, so it stays neutral and works as a cooking medium. Kitchens also hold it hotter than a beurre blanc, 70 to 85°C (158 to 185°F) against 55 to 60°C (131 to 140°F); the figures are kitchen practice, so follow the chef and the thermometer.

It splits when it boils, when it is left to cool and then reheated fast, or when water evaporates over a long hold until too little remains to carry the fat. The sign is always the same: a clear layer of fat over a thin, milky one. A bath that has grown thick and tight is caught early by whisking in a splash of hot water. A bath that has fully separated is split butter, fat over milky water, not clarified butter, which has had its water and milk solids taken away. A small batch can be whisked back slowly into a spoonful of fresh hot water; a large poaching bath is better made again.

Through service, keep it in a bain-marie, a pan set in hot water, or in an insulated container at the back of the stove, and give it a whisk now and then. Make a fresh batch for each service rather than carrying one over, and start again sooner whenever it splits, tastes scorched or has already poached something. A bath that has cooked lobster carries lobster, a shellfish, into whatever it touches next, a cross-contact risk as well as a flavour, so it stays with that one use, and allergen questions go to the kitchen. How long a batch stays on the station is the chef's call.
For the guest, say burr mohn-TAY and keep it simple: butter whisked with a little water so it stays creamy, used to cook lobster or fish gently.

entries.title: Beurre noisette and beurre noir
entries.summary: Brown butter: butter cooked until its milk solids toast to the colour of hazelnuts and it smells nutty, then stopped at once. Taken darker and sharpened with vinegar and capers, it is beurre noir. Seconds separate brown from burnt.
entries.guest: Brown butter, beurre noisette, is butter cooked until its milk solids toast golden and it smells nutty, warm and rich. Our Louisiana Crab Claws come in a warm brown butter vinaigrette.

paras: Beurre noisette means hazelnut butter, named for its colour and its smell; English-speaking kitchens call it brown butter. It is whole butter cooked past melting until its water boils away and the milk solids, the small white specks of protein and sugar in butter, toast golden brown on the bottom of the pan. The fat takes on their flavour: nutty, sweet, a little like toffee. It is one of the simplest sauces in French cooking and one of the quickest to ruin.

Beurre noir, black butter, is the same butter taken a shade darker and sharpened with vinegar, classically with capers, for skate and for brains. The name overstates it: butter that is truly black is burnt, bitter and acrid, and no good kitchen serves it. A proper beurre noir is a deep, dark brown.

Use a light-coloured pan, stainless steel rather than black iron or non-stick, so you can see the colour change. Cut the butter into pieces and melt it over medium heat. It foams and crackles loudly as its water boils off, about a sixth of its weight. Swirl the pan. When the water has gone, the crackling quietens, the foam subsides, the fat climbs past 100°C (212°F) and, from about 120°C (248°F), brown flecks appear on the bottom. Within moments the butter smells of toasted hazelnuts. For 115 g (4 oz) of butter the whole process takes four to six minutes.

Now stop it, at once. Pour it into a cool bowl, scraping in the brown specks, which carry the flavour; or add lemon juice or vinegar, standing back, because acid spits in hot fat; or add the food. Left in a hot pan the butter goes on cooking from the pan's heat, so experienced cooks pull it a shade before it looks ready. For beurre noir, take it a little further, to deep brown, then add a splash of vinegar off the heat and the capers.

Several classics are built on the same browned butter. À la grenobloise, in the style of Grenoble, adds capers, peeled lemon segments cut small and croûtons, small cubes of fried bread, usually spooned over fish. A brown butter vinaigrette whisks warm brown butter with an acid such as lemon juice or sherry vinegar, with salt and sometimes shallot, and is served warm, because the butterfat sets as it cools. In pastry, brown butter flavours madeleines and financiers. Meunière and amandine, the brown butter fish, are taught on their own.

Burnt butter cannot be saved: if the specks are black and it smells bitter or smoky, pour it away, wipe the pan and start again. Pale butter, stopped too soon, tastes only of melted butter. A dark pan hides the colour until it is too late. And clarified butter will never turn nutty, because the milk solids that do the browning have been taken out.

At Brennan's brown butter works in three ways. On the Louisiana Crab Claws it becomes a warm brown butter vinaigrette, sharpened with acid and finished with fines herbes, feen ZAIRB, the French mix of parsley, chives, tarragon and chervil, and the claws are served warm. In the Turtle Soup, spinach is wilted in brown butter, so it turns soft and nutty, and is folded through the soup under finely grated hard-boiled egg and a lift of aged sherry. In the Blackberry Trifle, the blackberry financiers, small buttery French cakes the guide calls biscuits, are made with brown butter, which gives them their rich, nutty flavour.

Say beurre noisette as burr nwah-ZET, or simply brown butter, and describe it as butter cooked until its milk solids toast and it smells nutty. Say aloud that the crab claws arrive warm, since many guests expect them cold, and bring napkins and a plate for the shells. Every allergen or dairy question goes to the kitchen and the service note.

cards.front: What does beurre noisette mean, and why?
cards.back: Hazelnut butter: the toasted milk solids turn it hazelnut brown and make it smell of toasted hazelnuts. In English, brown butter.

cards.front: Which part of the butter actually browns?
cards.back: The milk solids, small specks of protein and sugar, which sink and toast once the water has boiled away.

cards.front: What are the cues, in order, as butter browns?
cards.back: It melts and foams loudly, the foam subsides and the crackling quietens, brown flecks appear, then it smells of toasted hazelnuts.

cards.front: How do you stop brown butter before it burns?
cards.back: At once: pour it into a cool bowl, add lemon or vinegar, or add the food. Left in the hot pan it keeps cooking.

cards.front: Why brown butter in a light-coloured pan?
cards.back: So you can see the colour; a dark or non-stick pan hides the browning until the butter has burnt.

cards.front: What is beurre noir, classically?
cards.back: Butter taken to a deep, dark brown and sharpened with vinegar, usually with capers, served with skate or brains.

cards.front: Is beurre noir really black?
cards.back: No. Truly black butter is burnt, bitter and acrid; a proper beurre noir is a deep, dark brown.

cards.front: What makes a fish à la grenobloise?
cards.back: Brown butter with capers, peeled lemon segments and croûtons, small cubes of fried bread, spooned over the fish.

cards.front: Why is a brown butter vinaigrette served warm?
cards.back: Brown butter sets as it cools; warm, it stays liquid and coats food in a glossy film, with the acid cutting its richness.

cards.front: Why will clarified butter never turn nutty brown?
cards.back: Its milk solids have been removed, and they are what toasts and gives brown butter its nutty flavour.

entries.title: À la meunière
entries.summary: The miller's wife's way with fish: seasoned, dusted in flour and sautéed golden in clarified butter, then dressed at the last moment with foaming brown butter, lemon juice and parsley. New Orleans kitchens make a richer brown sauce of their own.
entries.guest: Meunière means the miller's wife's way: fish dusted in flour, pan-fried golden in butter and finished with nutty brown butter, lemon and parsley.

paras: À la meunière means in the style of the miller's wife, a name that points at the flour. The fish, usually thin white fillets or a small flat fish, is seasoned, dusted in flour and sautéed, cooked quickly in a little hot fat, until golden on both sides. Then fresh butter is browned to noisette, hazelnut brown, in a clean pan, lemon juice and chopped parsley go in, and the foaming butter is poured straight over the fish.

The flour is the point. It browns into a thin, crisp skin that shields delicate flesh from the heat, keeps it moist and gives the butter something to cling to. It is the method behind sole meunière in France and trout meunière in New Orleans, and the base on which amandine is built.

Pat the fish dry with a cloth and season it with salt and white pepper. Heat clarified butter, enough to film the pan generously, in a heavy frying pan over medium-high heat until it shimmers. Clarified butter has had its milk solids removed, so it takes the heat without burning.

Only now dredge the fish, drawing it through a tray of plain flour, never ahead, or the flour turns to paste, and shake off every bit of excess: you want a veil, not a coat. Lay the fish in presentation side down, the side the guest will see, and leave it alone until the edge turns golden, about two to three minutes for a fillet 1 cm thick, less for thin sole. Turn it once, cook the second side and lift it onto a warm plate.

Pour off the fat and wipe out the pan, since scorched flour would make the sauce bitter. Add fresh whole butter, about 30 g (1 oz) a portion, and cook it to noisette, hazelnut brown and smelling of toasted nuts. Off the heat add 1 to 2 tsp (5 to 10 ml) of lemon juice, which makes it foam, and a spoonful of chopped parsley, then pour it foaming over the fish and send it at once.

Thin, white, delicate fish suit it: sole, flounder, trout, and on the Gulf, speckled trout and drum. In New Orleans, trout on a menu usually means speckled trout, the spotted seatrout of the Gulf's bays, not a freshwater fish. Thick or oily fish such as salmon or tuna gain little from a flour coat and a brown butter sauce.

The New Orleans meunière is a sauce of its own. The old Creole houses serve a richer, darker brown butter sauce, in some kitchens built with stock, Worcestershire sauce or a little brown roux, flour cooked in fat until brown, and sharpened with lemon. Recipes vary from house to house and each guards its own, so a cook learns the house version and a server describes the plate in front of them, not a textbook.

A soggy coat comes from wet fish, flour put on too early or a pan that was not hot enough, so the fish steamed instead of frying. Too much flour gives a thick, pasty crust that falls away. Burnt, bitter butter comes from browning the sauce with the fish still in the pan, or over scorched flour: brown the butter only once the fish is out and the pan is clean. A fillet that sticks and tears was turned before its crust had set.

Escoffier's Guide gives sole à la meunière much as it is made today: floured, cooked in butter, sprinkled with lemon juice and parsley and finished with butter cooked to noisette. In the English-speaking world it is best remembered as the sole meunière Julia Child ate at La Couronne in Rouen in 1948, the meal she credited with opening her eyes to French food.

Say muhn-YEHR. Describe it plainly: fish dusted in flour, pan-fried in butter and finished with brown butter, lemon and parsley. A meunière waits for nobody, since the coat softens and the butter stops foaming within minutes, so it goes from the pass, the counter where plates leave the kitchen, to the table straight away. The coat is flour, so a guest who asks about gluten or wheat is sent to the kitchen, never answered from memory.

entries.title: Amandine
entries.summary: Amandine is fish cooked the meunière way and finished with flaked almonds toasted golden in brown butter, with lemon and parsley. It is the method behind New Orleans's trout amandine, and the template for the Louisiana habit of putting pecans in the pan.
entries.guest: Amandine means finished with almonds: the fish is sautéed golden in butter, then topped with almonds toasted in brown butter, with lemon and parsley.

paras: Amandine, from the French amande, almond, is a finish rather than a sauce of its own. The fish is first cooked à la meunière, the miller's wife's way: seasoned, dusted in flour and sautéed golden. Then flaked almonds are toasted in fresh butter until the butter turns hazelnut brown and the almonds pale gold, lemon juice and chopped parsley go in at the last moment, and the foaming panful is spooned over the fish. The almonds bring crunch and a sweet, toasted flavour that a plain meunière lacks.

In New Orleans a favourite plate is trout amandine, made with speckled trout, a Gulf fish of the drum family rather than a freshwater trout. American menus often spell it almondine, an anglicised form of the French word. Both mean the same plate, and a cook should recognise either on a ticket.

Season the fillets, dredge them in flour and shake off every bit of excess. Sauté them in clarified butter, butter with its water and milk solids taken out so it takes the heat without burning, over medium-high heat until golden on both sides, a few minutes for a thin fillet, and lift them onto a warm plate. Pour off the fat and wipe the pan, or take a second one, because flour left behind burns as the butter browns.

Put the pan over medium heat with fresh whole butter. When it foams, add the almonds and keep them moving so every flake colours evenly. Within a minute or two the foam settles, the milk solids turn brown and the butter smells of hazelnuts; the almonds should be pale gold to light brown. Off the heat, add the lemon juice, which hisses and stops the browning, then the parsley and a pinch of salt. Spoon it over the fish at once, while it still foams.

Busy kitchens often toast the almonds ahead on a tray in the oven, at about 160 to 175°C (320 to 347°F) for 5 to 8 minutes, then warm them through in the browning butter to order. The nuts colour evenly and the line moves faster.

For one portion of 170 to 200 g (6 to 7 oz) of fish, allow about 30 g (1 oz) of butter for the sauce, 20 to 25 g (about 3/4 oz) of flaked almonds, 1 to 2 tsp (5 to 10 ml) of lemon juice and a spoonful of chopped parsley. Flaked almonds, cut thin, toast faster and more evenly than slivered or whole ones.

Almonds go from golden to burnt in seconds and keep cooking in the hot butter after the pan leaves the heat, so pull them a shade lighter than you want them. Burnt nuts taste bitter and cannot be saved: start again. A soggy coat on the fish comes from wet fillets, too much flour or a pan that was not hot enough. Black specks in the sauce are flour left from the sauté. Parsley added too early wilts and darkens, and butter left without its lemon goes on browning towards burnt.

The same logic works with other nuts. Louisiana cooks put pecans in the pan in exactly the same way, a toasted pecan butter spooned over sautéed or fried fish, and hazelnuts or pistachios turn up on modern menus. The method fits any thin, white, delicate fillet that takes a meunière well: sole, flounder, drum or trout.

No amandine appears on the menus the house guide covers. The nearest cousin is the Pecan Gulf Fish: today's Gulf fish with lump crab and a pecan bordelaise. In New Orleans bordelaise usually means garlic butter rather than the French red wine sauce, and the guide reads this one as garlic butter with toasted pecans worked in: nuts and butter over fish, the Louisiana swap. That is a reading, not a recipe, so confirm at lineup which bordelaise it is.

Describe amandine plainly: fish sautéed golden in butter, with almonds toasted in brown butter, lemon and parsley spooned over. Almonds are tree nuts and they toast in the same butter that sauces the fish, so a nut allergy question goes straight to the kitchen, which alone decides whether a separate, clean pan and fresh butter are possible. Never promise it yourself.

entries.title: Clarified butter
entries.summary: Clarified butter is butter with its water and milk solids taken away, leaving pure golden butterfat. It takes more heat than whole butter without burning, gives a firmer hollandaise and is the cooking fat of a meunière.
entries.guest: Clarified butter is butter melted gently and strained so only the pure golden fat remains; it gives fish a clean, buttery crust without burning.

paras: Butter is not all fat. American butter must by law be at least 80 per cent butterfat; most of the rest is water, about 16 per cent, with a little milk protein, milk sugar and sometimes salt, together called the milk solids. Clarifying separates them. Melted gently, the water cooks away or settles, the solids rise as foam or sink, and what remains is clear, golden butterfat, beurre clarifié in French.

It matters because the milk solids are what burn. Whole butter starts to smoke and scorch at around 150 to 175°C (302 to 347°F); clarified butter holds to roughly 200 to 250°C (392 to 482°F), the figure varying with the source and with how cleanly the butter was clarified. With no water left it does not spit in a hot pan, and it keeps far longer than whole butter.

Cooks reach for it in three places. It is the fat for sautéing fish à la meunière and anything else cooked hot in butter, because it browns the food without burning itself. It makes a thicker, steadier hollandaise than whole butter, which brings its own water. And with nothing to spit or scorch, it suits the crêpe pan and the pastry brush.

Use unsalted butter, so the seasoning stays in the cook's hands. Cut it into pieces and melt it over low heat, in a heavy pan, a bain-marie (a pan set in hot water) or a low oven. Let it bubble quietly without stirring: the water cooks off with a soft crackle, and a white foam of milk protein rises. Skim it away.

When the bubbling slows and the fat looks clear, take it off the heat and let it stand a few minutes. Ladle or pour the golden fat off the top, leave the milky layer at the bottom behind, and strain it through muslin (cheesecloth) for a clean finish. Another way: melt it, chill it until the fat sets into a disc, lift the disc off and discard the liquid beneath.
Expect about 75 to 80 per cent of the weight you started with: 450 g (1 lb) of butter gives roughly 340 to 360 g (about 12 oz) of clarified butter. Plan the order for that loss.

Ghee is the clarified butter of South Asian kitchens, taken one step further. The butter is cooked on after the water has gone, until the milk solids on the bottom turn golden brown and the fat smells nutty and toasted, then it is strained. It tastes deeper than plain clarified butter and is the everyday fat for frying spices, cooking rice and brushing breads. Because the browned solids are strained out, it is a cousin of brown butter, not the same thing.

Cloudy clarified butter still holds milk solids: let it settle and decant it again, more slowly, through muslin. Fat that spits still holds water and needed longer over the heat. If the heat was too high the solids brown and the fat tastes nutty, which suits some dishes but not a pale hollandaise. Clarified salted butter leaves most of its salt in the milky layer, but some carries over, so taste before seasoning.

On the station, clarified butter is kept liquid in a covered container or squeeze bottle in a warm spot, such as the back of the stove, with its own clean ladle. Flour from dredged fish, crumbs and used pan fat never go back in: they burn the next time the butter heats and spoil the whole batch. Label and date it, and follow the chef's rule for how long it stays out.

Guests meet it as drawn butter, the warm melted or clarified butter American menus serve with lobster, crab and steamed clams, and in the clean, golden crust of a meunière. A guest who asks whether clarified butter or ghee is still dairy is answered by the kitchen and the service note, never by a guess: both are made from butter.

entries.title: Compound butters
entries.summary: Compound butters, beurres composés in French, are softened butter worked with a flavouring, rolled, chilled and sliced. A disc melts over hot grilled meat or fish into an instant sauce; others, such as crustacean butter, finish classic sauces.
entries.guest: A compound butter is butter blended with herbs or other flavourings, chilled and sliced, so it melts over the hot food into a quick, rich sauce.

paras: A compound butter, beurre composé in French, is softened butter beaten with a flavouring, rolled into a log, chilled and sliced. A cold disc laid on a hot grilled steak or fish melts into a glossy, seasoned sauce on the way to the table, with no pan and no last-minute work. Escoffier listed a long run of them, some for grills and some for finishing sauces, and those two uses still divide the family.
For a Sous Chef they are mise en place, the work set out before service, that becomes a sauce: made in a quiet hour, sliced to order, and the same on the last plate as on the first.

Bring unsalted butter to a soft, spreadable texture, about 18 to 20°C (64 to 68°F), what French cooks call en pommade: soft enough to take a fingertip, nowhere near melting. Beat it smooth, then work in the flavourings, chopped fine and dry, then salt and pepper, and any acid last, a little at a time so the butter takes the liquid. Keep wet additions such as a reduction modest, or the butter weeps.

Spoon the butter in a line along parchment or cling film (plastic wrap), roll it into a tight cylinder about 3 cm (about 1 1/4 inches) across, twist the ends and chill until firm. Slice discs to order with a knife dipped in hot water and dried, or freeze the logs and cut from frozen.

Crustacean butter, beurre de crustacés, is the exception, often made hot. The shells of lobster, crayfish or shrimp are pounded or blitzed with butter and heated gently until the fat turns coral red and smells of the sea, then strained through cloth into iced water, where the coloured fat sets and is lifted off. It finishes sauce Nantua, béchamel (milk thickened with a roux of butter and flour) enriched with cream and finished with crayfish butter and crayfish tails, and sauce cardinal, which owes its red colour to lobster butter.

Maître d'hôtel butter is the classic: parsley, lemon juice, salt and pepper, on grilled steak and grilled fish. Bercy butter adds shallot reduced in white wine and diced, poached beef marrow, with parsley and lemon, for grilled steak. Colbert butter is maître d'hôtel butter with melted meat glaze, glace de viande, and chopped tarragon. Escargot butter, packed over snails in their shells and baked, is garlic, shallot and parsley beaten into butter.

Then there are house butters. Café de Paris butter takes its name from the Café de Paris in Geneva, which serves entrecôte, a rib steak, beneath it and still keeps the recipe secret; versions made elsewhere run to a long list of herbs, spices, mustard and capers. Many restaurants keep a signature butter of their own.

Butter too cold will not take its flavourings and stays lumpy and streaked. Butter too warm, or melted, turns greasy, the herbs sink and it sets grainy when chilled again. Wet herbs or a warm reduction weep beads of water and shorten the butter's life, so dry the herbs and cool every liquid first. Garlic and fresh herbs fade within days: keep the logs wrapped, labelled, dated and cold, and freeze what will not be used soon.

At Brennan's two compound butters finish dishes on the breakfast and lunch menu. Foie gras butter, foie gras puréed into soft butter, melts into the pockets of the cornbread waffle on the Duck Confit Waffle with the mustard maple syrup. House-made miso butter is miso, a fermented soybean paste, beaten into soft butter, salty, nutty and savoury; it rounds out the sweet crab and corn on the Crab & Corn Omelette, and because the guide names soy on this dish, dietary questions go to the service note and the kitchen.

Describe a compound butter by what is in it and what it does: herbs and lemon melting over a steak, foie gras melting into a waffle. Some guests avoid foie gras by choice, and the house guide asks you to check with the kitchen whether it can be left off before you promise it. Crustacean butter in a sauce, miso in a butter: every question about what a butter is made with goes to the service note and the kitchen.

entries.title: Mayonnaise
entries.summary: Mayonnaise is a cold emulsion of egg yolk and oil, seasoned with mustard and sharpened with vinegar or lemon. It is the cold cousin of hollandaise and the parent of rémoulade, tartare, verte and a family of cold sauces.
entries.guest: Mayonnaise is egg yolk whisked with oil, a little mustard and lemon or vinegar into a thick, cool sauce, the base of tartare sauce and the French rémoulade.

paras: Mayonnaise is a cold emulsion: tiny droplets of oil held apart in a little water, from the yolk and the vinegar or lemon juice. Lecithin and proteins in the yolk coat each droplet so the droplets cannot run back together, and their crowding is what makes the sauce thick. Mustard adds flavour and helps the emulsion form. No heat is involved: it is the cold cousin of hollandaise.

Escoffier treated it as a basic sauce, the parent of the cold sauces, doing for the cold kitchen what espagnole, the brown sauce, and velouté, the white stock sauce, do for the hot one. It is not among the four grandes sauces de base, the great base sauces, of his Guide (espagnole, velouté, béchamel and tomate), nor among the five mother sauces that later teaching made by adding hollandaise, but it stands beside them.

Have everything at room temperature: a cold yolk is slow to emulsify, and cold oil is thick and hard to break into droplets. Set the bowl on a damp cloth to steady it and whisk the yolk with the mustard, a pinch of salt and a few drops of vinegar or lemon juice.

Add the oil a drop at a time, whisking all the while, until the sauce thickens and turns pale: the emulsion has taken. Then pour in a thin, steady stream. As it stiffens, whisk in a few drops of water or lemon juice before adding more oil, because what runs out first is the water, not the yolk. Finish with acid and salt to taste. A food processor or stick blender works the same way, only faster.

Use a neutral oil such as sunflower, rapeseed (canola) or grapeseed. Olive oil brings flavour, but extra virgin olive oil beaten hard, above all in a blender, can turn bitter, so cooks use it for only part of the oil, whisked in by hand at the end.

One yolk comfortably holds roughly 150 to 250 ml of oil, with about 1 tsp (5 ml) of mustard and 1 to 2 tsp (5 to 10 ml) of vinegar or lemon juice. Escoffier worked at six yolks to 1 litre (about 1 quart) of oil, about 165 ml a yolk. A yolk can carry far more if water goes in as it thickens, but a working ratio leaves a margin.

From mayonnaise come rémoulade, with mustard, gherkins, capers, herbs and a little anchovy; tartare, today usually mayonnaise with chopped pickles, capers, onion and chives, though the classical one was mounted on hard-boiled yolks; verte, coloured green with a purée of blanched herbs and leaves such as spinach, watercress, tarragon and chervil; and andalouse, with tomato purée and fine strips of sweet red pepper. Aïoli and the New Orleans rémoulades, some built on mayonnaise and some on Creole mustard without it, have entries of their own.

A mayonnaise splits, turning thin, oily and curdled, when the oil goes in too fast before the emulsion has taken, when the ingredients are cold, or when too much oil is forced into too little water. To rescue it, put a fresh yolk, or a spoonful of water or mustard, in a clean bowl and whisk the broken sauce into it drop by drop, then in a stream. A sauce that is only too thick needs a few drops of water, not more oil.

The yolk in a mayonnaise is never cooked, and Salmonella can be inside an egg as well as on its shell. Restaurant kitchens therefore commonly make it with pasteurised eggs or yolks, heated just enough to kill bacteria without setting. Keep mayonnaise and everything made from it covered and cold, at 5°C (41°F) or below, and follow the kitchen's dating.

At the table, say what it is: egg yolk and oil whisked into a cool, thick sauce. What goes into any house sauce is the kitchen's answer, never a guess: the style of the chive rémoulade on the Crawfish Meat Pies is the kitchen's to say, as is any question about egg in a sauce.

entries.title: Aïoli and the French rémoulade
entries.summary: Aïoli is the garlic sauce of Provence: garlic pounded with salt, olive oil worked in, usually with a yolk. The French rémoulade is mayonnaise with mustard, gherkins, capers, herbs and anchovy. Rouille, tartare and gribiche complete the family.
entries.guest: Aïoli is the garlic and olive oil sauce of Provence. Our Crawfish Meat Pies come with a chive rémoulade for dipping: cool, tangy and herby against the hot pastry.

paras: Aïoli and the French rémoulade are two pillars of the cold kitchen, each with a family around it. Aïoli, said eye-OH-lee, is the garlic sauce of Provence, and its name joins the Provençal words for garlic and oil. At its oldest it is nothing more: garlic pounded to a paste with coarse salt in a mortar, olive oil worked in drop by drop until it holds. Most kitchens now add an egg yolk, which makes it far steadier, so in practice it is a garlic mayonnaise made with olive oil.

In Provence, le grand aïoli is a whole meal built around the sauce: poached salt cod, boiled vegetables and hard-boiled eggs, all dipped in one big bowl. The French rémoulade, said REM-uh-lahd, is mayonnaise finished with mustard, chopped gherkins (small, sour pickled cucumbers), capers, herbs and a little anchovy: white, sharp and herby, for cold meats, fried fish and seafood.

For aïoli, pound 4 to 6 cloves of garlic with a good pinch of coarse salt to a smooth, sticky paste, pulling out any green shoot, which tastes harsh. Stir in one yolk and a few drops of water or lemon juice. Then mount it, meaning beat in the oil until the sauce thickens: about 250 ml (1 cup) of olive oil, a few drops at a time at first, then in a thin thread once it turns glossy. A peppery extra virgin oil can turn bitter beaten hard in a blender, so many cooks use half mild olive oil, or work by hand.

For the French rémoulade, start from a mayonnaise made with a neutral oil. To 250 ml (1 cup) of it add 1 tsp (5 ml) of Dijon mustard, 1 tbsp (15 ml) each of finely chopped gherkins and capers, squeezed dry in a cloth, 1 tbsp (15 ml) of chopped parsley, chervil and tarragon, and one anchovy fillet crushed to a paste. Rest it for half an hour and taste it cold.

Rouille, said roo-EE, French for rust, is aïoli's red cousin: garlic, chilli and a pinch of saffron pounded with bread soaked in fish broth, then mounted with olive oil, often with a yolk. It is spread on toasted bread and floated on bouillabaisse, the fish stew of Marseille.

Tartare and gribiche are the egg sauces. The classical French tartare was mounted not on raw yolks but on hard-boiled yolks pounded smooth, and finished with chives; most kitchens now make it as mayonnaise with gherkins, capers and herbs. Gribiche, said gree-BEESH, crushes hard-boiled yolks with mustard, mounts them with oil and folds in gherkins, capers, herbs and fine strips of the cooked whites, for cold fish and calf's head. Céleri rémoulade, the bistro salad, is raw celeriac cut into fine matchsticks in a sharp mustard mayonnaise.

The New Orleans rémoulade, taught as Creole rémoulade, kept the name and changed nearly everything: pink with paprika, hot with cayenne and horseradish, led by Creole mustard, sometimes with no mayonnaise at all. The French sauce is white, sharp and herby but never hot, led by its pickles and capers.

These sauces split as mayonnaise does, from oil added too fast or too cold. The rescue, a fresh yolk and patience, is taught with how emulsions break. Aïoli grows hotter and more bitter as it stands, so make it the day it is served. A rémoulade weeps when its gherkins and capers go in wet, and a gribiche turns grey and sulphurous when its eggs were boiled too long.

At Brennan's a chive rémoulade comes with the Crawfish Meat Pies, a snack on the Bubbles at Brennan's list in the Roost Bar. The house guide calls it cool, tangy and herby against the hot pastry. The menu does not print the recipe, so whether it leans French, white and herby, or New Orleans, pink and hot, is the kitchen's to say.

Describe aïoli as a garlic mayonnaise made with olive oil, and the French rémoulade as a white, herby mayonnaise with capers and pickles, close to tartare sauce. Most of these sauces are built on egg yolk and oil, but the house recipe is the kitchen's, so send every allergen question to the kitchen and the service note.

entries.title: Vinaigrette
entries.summary: Vinaigrette is oil and vinegar whisked into a temporary emulsion, classically three parts oil to one of acid, with salt, mustard and shallot dissolved in the acid first. Warm versions of bacon fat or brown butter coat leaves better.
entries.guest: A vinaigrette is a dressing of oil and vinegar, whisked with mustard and shallot. Our Louisiana Crab Claws come warm in a brown butter vinaigrette, nutty and bright.

paras: A vinaigrette is one of the simplest sauces in the cold kitchen and one of the most used: oil and an acid, usually vinegar, seasoned and whisked so the oil breaks into tiny droplets through the vinegar. Left alone it separates within minutes, because nothing strong holds the droplets apart. That makes it a temporary emulsion, an emulsion being fat held in droplets through a watery liquid, and it is why a vinaigrette is whisked or shaken again just before use. A little mustard slows the parting: its fine particles and natural gums coat the droplets and keep the dressing creamy for longer.
The name comes from vinaigre, vinegar, which itself means sour wine. Beyond leaves, it dresses leeks, asparagus, boiled potatoes, lentils, grilled fish and cold meats.

The classic ratio is three parts oil to one of vinegar by volume: 180 ml (3/4 cup) of oil to 60 ml (1/4 cup) of vinegar dresses about eight salads. Put the vinegar in a bowl with a good pinch of salt, 1 tsp (5 ml) of Dijon mustard and 1 tbsp (15 ml) of finely chopped shallot, and leave it for five minutes. Salt dissolves in vinegar but not in oil, and the acid softens the shallot's raw bite. Whisk in the oil in a slow stream until the dressing thickens slightly and turns opaque, then add pepper.

Taste it on a leaf, not from a spoon: neat, every dressing tastes harsh, and the leaves soften it, so a dressing balanced on the spoon eats flat and oily on the salad. On its own it should taste a touch too sharp and salty. A sharp acid such as lemon juice may want four parts oil; a mellow Champagne or cane vinegar can take a little less.

Dress leaves at the last moment, in a wide bowl, with a little dressing, turning them until every leaf shines and nothing pools on the plate. The leaves must be dry, because water repels oil and thins the dressing, and acid and salt wilt tender leaves within minutes, so a dressed salad cannot wait. Potatoes, lentils and leeks are the exception: dressed warm, they drink it in.

The acid sets the character. Red wine vinegar is robust, for bitter leaves and beef; white wine vinegar is clean and does everything; sherry vinegar is nutty and deep, for walnuts, mushrooms and warm dressings; Champagne vinegar is light and delicate, for soft leaves and seafood; Louisiana cane vinegar, made from sugar cane, is mild with a soft sweetness; lemon juice is fresh but fades within hours.

Warm vinaigrettes swap some or all of the oil for a warm fat. Bacon fat, rendered from lardons (small batons of bacon) and sharpened with vinegar in the same pan, dresses the frisée, the curly, bitter endive, of a Lyonnaise salad. Brown butter is whisked with acid into a nutty dressing; brown butter itself is taught with beurre noisette. Warm dressings coat better because warm fat is thinner and flows into every fold of a leaf, and the warmth softens sturdy greens so they take the dressing in.

A dressing that separates was not whisked hard enough or has no mustard; whisk it again just before use. One that tastes harsh even on a leaf has too much acid, or salt stirred into the oil, where it never dissolves. A warm vinaigrette gone thick and cloudy has simply cooled, and butter and bacon fat set: warm it gently, whisk and serve at once.

At Brennan's the Louisiana Crab Claws come warm in a brown butter vinaigrette: butter browned until nutty, sharpened with acid so it is rich but bright, with fines herbes, feen ZAIRB, the classic French mix of parsley, chives, tarragon and chervil, tossed through at the last moment. The house guide does not name the acid, so ask the kitchen before naming it to a guest.

Say vin-uh-GRET and describe it plainly as a dressing of oil and vinegar. For the claws, say warm brown butter vinaigrette, nutty and bright, and say warm aloud, because many guests expect cold claws. Questions about what is in any dressing, mustard or anything else, go to the kitchen and the service note.

entries.title: Mignonette
entries.say: min-yo-NET (meen-yo-NET, nearer the French, is also heard)
entries.summary: Mignonette is the raw oyster’s sauce: finely chopped shallot in red wine or Champagne vinegar with coarsely cracked black pepper. A spoonful lifts the oyster’s brine without drowning it; ours adds preserved Fresno chilli and parsley.
entries.guest: Mignonette is the classic raw oyster sauce: shallot, cracked pepper and vinegar. Ours adds preserved Fresno chilli and parsley, a gentle warmth on the Grand Isle Jewel oysters.

paras: Mignonette, said min-yo-NET, is the sauce of the raw bar: shallot chopped very fine and steeped in red wine or Champagne vinegar with coarsely cracked black pepper. A raw oyster tastes of salt and the sea; a few drops of sharp vinegar, sweet shallot and the warmth of pepper lift that brine and clean the palate between oysters. It is one of the simplest sauces a Commis will make, and one of the most exact, because it sits beside one of the most delicate things on the menu.

The name comes from the pepper. In French kitchens mignonnette, spelt with two n's, is the old name for peppercorns coarsely cracked rather than ground to dust, and the sauce is named after it. That is its first lesson: crack the pepper, never powder it.

Cut one large shallot, about 40 g (1.5 oz), into the finest brunoise you can manage, tiny even dice of 1 to 2 mm, so each spoonful carries sweet shallot without a crunch of raw onion. Put it in a small bowl with 120 ml (1/2 cup) of red wine vinegar or Champagne vinegar. Crack 1 tsp (5 ml) of black peppercorns coarsely in a mortar or under the base of a heavy pan and stir them in; ready-ground pepper turns the vinegar muddy. Salt is optional, because the oyster brings its own.

Cover it and chill it for at least 30 minutes, so the shallot softens and gives the vinegar its sweetness. Make it fresh each day: after a day or two the shallot goes soft and grey and the sauce tastes flat.

Red wine vinegar gives a robust, pink sauce; Champagne vinegar a paler, gentler one for the most delicate oysters. Variations add finely grated lemon or lime zest, cucumber cut as fine as the shallot for coolness, fresh or preserved chilli for warmth, or chopped parsley or chives. Each stays a seasoning: a few drops of sharp, clean flavour, not a salsa.

At a New Orleans oyster bar the raw oyster more often meets cocktail sauce and hot sauce. Many New Orleans oyster bars hand guests ketchup, horseradish, lemon and hot sauce to mix their own cocktail sauce. Mignonette is the French-leaning choice, lighter and sharper than either, and the one that lets the oyster taste most of itself.

A spoonful, not a flood. Poured over ahead of time, the acid starts to firm the oyster, and too much drowns the brine the guest came for. Coarsely cut shallot crunches and takes over; finely ground pepper muddies the vinegar; a batch made days ahead tastes tired. A fierce vinegar is better swapped for a gentler one than watered down.

At Brennan's the Grand Isle Jewel oysters, a dinner starter and the first course of the dinner tasting, are served raw on the half shell with a preserved Fresno chilli mignonette and parsley. The Fresno is a red chilli about as hot as a jalapeño but fruitier; preserved, salted or pickled, and diluted in the vinegar, it reads as a gentle, fruity warmth rather than real heat, which is why the service note calls it mild. How the chilli is preserved, and which vinegar the kitchen uses, are questions for the chef. One of the ten courtyard turtles is named Mignonette.

Say min-yo-NET, as the house guide does; meen-yo-NET, nearer the French, is also heard. Describe it as shallot, cracked pepper and vinegar, and ours as made with preserved Fresno chilli for a gentle warmth. The house guide says the guest spoons it onto each oyster at the table; it is never poured over in advance, so set it beside the oysters and show a first-timer how little to use. These oysters are raw, so give the consumer advisory the service note asks for: raw oysters carry a risk of illness, above all for guests who are pregnant, immunocompromised or have liver disease. Send every question about raw seafood to the kitchen or the manager.

cards.front: How fine should the shallot be cut, and why?
cards.back: A very fine brunoise, tiny even dice of 1 to 2 mm, so each spoonful carries sweet shallot without a crunch of raw onion.

cards.front: Why crack the peppercorns rather than use ready-ground pepper?
cards.back: Cracked pepper gives clean bursts of warmth; finely ground pepper turns the vinegar muddy and dusty.

cards.front: How long should a mignonette rest, and how long does it keep?
cards.back: At least 30 minutes, covered and chilled, so the shallot softens and sweetens the vinegar; make it fresh each day.

cards.front: How much mignonette goes on a raw oyster?
cards.back: A few drops to half a teaspoon: enough to lift the brine, never enough to drown it.

cards.front: Why is mignonette spooned on at the table rather than poured over in advance?
cards.back: Its acid starts to firm the oyster, so the guest adds it just before eating, as the house guide says.

cards.front: What else sits beside raw oysters at a New Orleans oyster bar?
cards.back: Cocktail sauce, often stirred by the guest from ketchup, horseradish, lemon and Louisiana hot sauce.

cards.front: What is in the mignonette on Brennan’s Grand Isle Jewel oysters?
cards.back: Preserved Fresno chilli and parsley with the shallot, pepper and vinegar: a gentle, fruity warmth rather than real heat.

cards.front: How hot is the Fresno chilli in our mignonette?
cards.back: About as hot as a jalapeño but fruitier; preserved and diluted in vinegar it reads as a gentle warmth, which is why the service note calls it mild.

cards.front: How does the house guide say mignonette?
cards.back: The house guide writes min-yo-NET; meen-yo-NET, nearer the French, is also heard at the table.

cards.front: What does the service note ask a server to give with the raw Grand Isle Jewel oysters?
cards.back: The consumer advisory on raw oysters. Questions about raw seafood go to the kitchen or the manager; a server never answers them alone.

questions.answer: Shallot, vinegar and cracked pepper

questions.why: Mignonette is shallot steeped in vinegar with cracked pepper; ketchup and horseradish make cocktail sauce instead.

A small French oyster

Warmed and ladled over like a butter sauce

Ground pepper has no heat at all
Cracking stops the pepper floating

In coarse chunks, for crunch
Puréed smooth in a blender

entries.title: How emulsions hold, break and come back
entries.say: As it reads: how emulsions hold, break and come back.
entries.summary: An emulsion is fat held in tiny droplets through water, or water through fat, by an emulsifier such as yolk, butter’s milk proteins or mustard. Heat, cold and haste break it; warm water, a fresh yolk or cold butter usually brings it back.
entries.guest: Hollandaise, béarnaise and beurre blanc are warm butter sauces: butter whisked into warm egg yolk or a sharp wine reduction until silky. They are delicate, so each comes to the table just warm.

paras: An emulsion is two liquids that will not mix, fat and water, persuaded into one smooth sauce. One is broken into droplets far too small to see and scattered through the other. In mayonnaise, hollandaise and beurre blanc, fat is scattered through a little water, lemon juice or reduction: an oil-in-water emulsion. Butter itself is the other way round, droplets of water held in fat, a water-in-oil emulsion, which is why it feels greasy rather than wet.

Left alone, droplets of fat find each other and pool. What stops them is an emulsifier, a molecule with one end that likes water and one that likes fat, which coats each droplet like a skin. Egg yolk is the great one: its lecithin and proteins hold mayonnaise and hollandaise. In a butter sauce the milk proteins already in the butter do the work, which is why beurre blanc needs no yolk. Mustard helps too, which is why it steadies a vinaigrette.

Warm emulsions break three ways. Too hot, and a yolk sauce scrambles: past about 70°C (158°F) the yolk proteins set into tiny curds, while a butter sauce pushed well past its working window loses its hold and the butterfat oils out in a clear, greasy layer. Too cool, sinking towards body heat, and the butterfat begins to set, so the sauce thickens, dulls and splits if it is rewarmed in a hurry. Too much fat too fast, and the emulsifier cannot coat droplets as quickly as they arrive, so they run together.

Cold emulsions break for mirror reasons. Oil added too fast, above all at the start, swamps the yolk before it has made any droplets. Too much oil for the yolk crowds the droplets until there is too little water to hold them: the sauce turns stiff and glassy, then suddenly greasy and thin. A cold bowl or cold oil makes the oil thick and slow to break into droplets, and a greasy bowl adds fat before the yolk is ready. Ingredients at room temperature and a clean, dry bowl prevent most breaks.

Most broken emulsions come back if you rebuild them a droplet at a time. Watch for the warning: a sauce that tightens, turns glassy or shows a sheen of fat at the edge is close to breaking, and a spoonful of warm water whisked straight in usually saves it. For a sauce split into a greasy pool, put a teaspoon of warm water or a fresh yolk in a clean bowl and whisk the broken sauce into it a few drops at a time, then in a thin stream once it takes. The fresh base gives the fat somewhere to go.
For hollandaise, first whisk the fresh yolk with a spoonful of water over barely simmering water to a light ribbon; a raw, cold yolk leaves the sauce thin.

For a beurre blanc starting to oil out from heat, take it off the stove and whisk in a cube or two of cold butter: the cold lowers the temperature and the new butter brings fresh milk proteins. If it has fully separated, warm a spoonful of reduction or cream in a clean pan and whisk the broken sauce back in slowly.

Know when to stop. A hollandaise or béarnaise that has truly scrambled, with visible curds of cooked egg, does not come back: heat has cooked the yolk, and no whisking will uncook it. Start a new batch.

Every cook breaks a sauce; the good ones say so at once. On the line a broken sauce is a calm moment, not a crisis: tell the chef, keep it off the plate, and rescue it or start again. A sauce that looks oily or grainy at the pass, the counter where plates leave the kitchen, goes back to the cook, never to the guest.

For servers, this explains the house's warm sauces: the hollandaise on the Eggs Hussarde and Eggs Owen, the béarnaise on the Creole-Spiced Hanger Steak and the beurre blanc on the Redfish Véronique are all warm emulsions. The house guide's warning about hollandaise says it in a line: too hot and it scrambles, too cool and it splits.

faults.fix: Whisk the broken sauce drop by drop into a fresh yolk or a teaspoon of warm water in a clean bowl.

faults.cause: Held too hot, so the emulsion loosened and the butterfat ran together.
faults.fix: Off the heat, whisk in a cube or two of cold butter; if fully split, whisk it slowly into warm reduction or cream.

faults.cause: Allowed to cool until the butterfat began to set.
faults.fix: Warm it very gently while whisking; never blast it with heat.

faults.cause: Too little water left for the fat it carries.
faults.fix: Whisk in a spoonful of warm water at once, before it splits.

faults.fix: If only just grainy, whisk in cold water off the heat and strain; if truly scrambled, start again.

cards.front: What is an emulsion, in kitchen terms?
cards.back: Two liquids that will not mix, fat and water, with one broken into tiny droplets and held through the other by an emulsifier.

cards.front: How do oil-in-water and water-in-oil emulsions differ? Give an example of each.
cards.back: Oil-in-water scatters fat through water, as in mayonnaise and hollandaise; water-in-oil scatters water through fat, as in butter itself.

cards.front: Name three emulsifiers a cook relies on.
cards.back: The lecithin and proteins in egg yolk, the milk proteins already in butter, and mustard, whose particles and gums coat the droplets.

cards.front: What happens when a warm emulsion gets too hot?
cards.back: A yolk sauce scrambles into grainy curds past about 70°C (158°F); a butter sauce loses its hold and oils out in a clear, greasy layer.

cards.front: What happens when a butter sauce gets too cool?
cards.back: The butterfat begins to set, so the sauce thickens and dulls, and it splits if it is rewarmed in a hurry rather than gently, while whisking.

cards.front: Why do cold emulsions such as mayonnaise break?
cards.back: Oil added too fast, too much oil for the yolk, or a cold bowl and cold oil that will not break into droplets.

cards.front: Why does too much oil for one yolk break a mayonnaise?
cards.back: The droplets crowd until too little water is left to go round; the sauce turns stiff and glassy, then suddenly greasy.

cards.front: What warns you that an emulsion is about to break?
cards.back: It tightens and turns glassy, or a sheen of fat appears at the edge; a spoonful of warm water whisked in then usually saves it.

cards.front: How do you rescue a split mayonnaise or hollandaise?
cards.back: Put a fresh yolk or a teaspoon of warm water in a clean bowl and whisk the broken sauce in drop by drop, then in a thin stream. For a hollandaise, first whisk the yolk with a spoonful of water over gentle heat to a ribbon.

cards.front: How do you save a beurre blanc that is starting to oil out from heat?
cards.back: Take it off the stove and whisk in a cube or two of cold butter: the cold lowers the heat and the butter adds fresh milk proteins.

cards.front: When is a broken sauce beyond rescue?
cards.back: When a yolk sauce has truly scrambled into curds: heat has cooked the egg, and no whisking uncooks it. Start a new batch.

cards.front: What should a cook do the moment a sauce breaks on the line?
cards.back: Say so at once, keep it off the plate, set the broken batch aside and rescue it or start again; it is a lesson, not a crisis.

questions.q: Butter itself is which kind of emulsion?
questions.answer: Water held in droplets through fat
distractors: Fat held in droplets through water
Air held in bubbles through cream
Not an emulsion at all, but pure fat
questions.why: Butter is water held in fat, which is why it feels greasy rather than wet; mayonnaise and hollandaise are the other way round, fat held in water.

questions.q: In a mayonnaise, what coats each oil droplet so the droplets cannot merge?
questions.answer: Lecithin and proteins from the yolk
distractors: Salt dissolved in the vinegar
Fine particles of cracked black pepper
Gelatine from the egg white
questions.why: Yolk lecithin and proteins have one end that likes water and one that likes fat, so they skin each droplet and hold the sauce.

questions.q: A hollandaise has turned grainy, with tiny specks through it. What has happened?
questions.answer: The yolk proteins have set into curds
distractors: The butter went in too fast
The lemon juice has soured the butter
The salt has drawn the fat out
questions.why: Past about 70°C (158°F) yolk proteins cook and set, so the smooth sauce turns into tiny curds.

questions.q: A beurre blanc left at the side of the stove has thickened and turned dull. Why?
questions.answer: The butterfat has begun to set
distractors: The shallot has soaked up the butter
The vinegar has evaporated away
The sauce has started to boil
questions.why: As a butter sauce cools towards body heat its fat starts to set, and it will split when warmed again unless warmed gently.

questions.q: Which mistake most often breaks a mayonnaise at the very start?
questions.answer: Adding the oil too fast
distractors: Using a yolk at room temperature
Whisking in only one direction
Adding a little mustard first
questions.why: At the start the yolk has made no droplets yet, so a rush of oil swamps it; the first oil goes in a few drops at a time.

questions.q: Why does too much oil for one yolk break a mayonnaise?
questions.answer: The water runs out
distractors: The yolk starts to cook in the oil
The oil turns bitter and sour
The salt can no longer dissolve
questions.why: The droplets crowd until the water runs out, so the sauce turns stiff and glassy, then suddenly greasy.

questions.q: To rebuild a split hollandaise on a fresh yolk, what is done to that yolk first?
questions.answer: Whisked with water to a light ribbon
distractors: Used raw and cold, straight from the fridge
Beaten with a spoonful of flour
Boiled until it sets firm
questions.why: A raw, cold yolk leaves the rebuilt sauce thin; whisked with a spoonful of water over barely simmering water to a ribbon, it is ready to take the broken sauce.

questions.q: A beurre blanc is starting to oil out from too much heat. What do you do first?
questions.answer: Off the heat, whisk in cold butter
distractors: Turn the heat up to bind it
Add a yolk and bring it to a boil
Whisk in a spoonful of flour
questions.why: Cold butter lowers the temperature and brings fresh milk proteins, so the sauce can take hold again.

questions.q: Which broken sauce cannot be rescued and must be made again?
questions.answer: A hollandaise scrambled into curds
distractors: A mayonnaise split from fast oil
A beurre blanc set from cold
A vinaigrette that has separated
questions.why: Scrambled yolk is cooked egg and cannot be uncooked; the other three come back with warm water, a fresh yolk, gentle heat or a whisk.

steps.title: Mount a beurre blanc
steps.prompt: Put the stages of a classic beurre blanc in order. One stage does not belong.
steps: Boil the white wine, white wine vinegar and chopped shallot until about 2 tbsp (30 ml) of syrupy liquid remains
If the house uses cream, add a spoonful now and reduce it by half
Turn the heat to its lowest, with the butter cold from the fridge in 2 cm cubes
Whisk in two or three cubes and let them soften into a creamy sauce
Add two more cubes as each lot turns creamy, lifting the pan whenever it feels hot
Season with salt, white pepper and a little lemon, and strain out the shallot or leave it in for a rustic sauce
Hold it warm, 55 to 60°C (131 to 140°F), in a bain-marie or at the back of the stove
steps.distractor: Whisk two egg yolks into the reduction to bind the butter
steps.why: The reduction is boiled down hard first, with any cream reduced in it, and only then does the heat drop. Cold butter goes in a few cubes at a time so each lot emulsifies before the next. A beurre blanc takes no yolk: the butter's own milk proteins hold it.

steps.title: Clarify butter
steps.prompt: Put the stages of clarifying butter in order. One stage does not belong.
steps: Cut unsalted butter into pieces
Melt it over low heat in a heavy pan, a bain-marie or a low oven
Let it bubble quietly without stirring while the water cooks off, skimming away the white foam of milk protein as it rises
When the bubbling slows and the fat looks clear, take it off the heat and let it stand
Ladle the golden fat off the top, leaving the milky layer behind
Strain it through muslin (cheesecloth) for a clean finish
Label and date it, and keep it liquid on the station with its own clean ladle
steps.distractor: Turn the heat up high and stir hard so the water boils off faster
steps.why: Low, quiet heat lets the water cook off and the solids part from the fat without browning; stirring would mix them back in. The foam is skimmed as it rises, the fat settles before it is ladled off, and muslin catches the last specks.

steps.title: Cook a fish à la meunière
steps.prompt: Put the stages of a fish à la meunière in order, from the raw fillet to the pass. One stage does not belong.
steps: Pat the fish dry with a cloth and season it with salt and white pepper
With the fish dried and seasoned, heat clarified butter in a heavy frying pan until it shimmers
Once the fat shimmers, dredge the fish in flour and shake off every bit of excess
Lay it in presentation side down and leave it until the edge turns golden
Turn it once, cook the second side and lift it onto a warm plate
Pour off the fat and wipe out the pan
Brown fresh whole butter to noisette, hazelnut brown and smelling of toasted nuts
Off the heat, add the lemon juice and chopped parsley
Pour the foaming butter over the fish and send it at once
steps.distractor: Brown the sauce butter around the fish while it finishes cooking, to save time
steps.why: The fish is dry and the fat shimmering before the flour goes on, so the coat fries crisp instead of turning to paste. The fish comes out and the pan is wiped before fresh butter browns, because scorched flour turns the sauce bitter; the lemon goes in off the heat.

steps.title: Make a mayonnaise by hand
steps.prompt: Put the stages of a mayonnaise whisked by hand in order. One stage does not belong.
steps: Have the yolk and the oil at room temperature, and set the bowl on a damp cloth
Whisk the yolk with the mustard, a pinch of salt and a few drops of vinegar or lemon juice
Whisk in the oil a drop at a time until the sauce thickens and turns pale
Once it has taken, pour the oil in a thin, steady stream, whisking all the while
When it stiffens, loosen it with a few drops of water or lemon juice, then whisk in the rest of the oil
Finish with acid and salt to taste
Cover it and keep it cold, at 5°C (41°F) or below
steps.distractor: Chill the bowl and the oil well first, so the sauce sets thicker
steps.why: The emulsion must take before the oil speeds up: drops first, until it turns pale and thick, then a stream. Water runs out before the yolk does, so a stiff sauce is loosened before more oil goes in. Cold ingredients slow the emulsion, so everything starts at room temperature.

steps.title: Rescue a split hollandaise
steps.prompt: A hollandaise has split on the line. Put the stages of the rescue in order. One stage does not belong.
steps: Take it off the heat and tell the chef at once
Look closely: a greasy split can be saved, but curds of cooked egg mean starting again
Put a teaspoon of warm water in a clean bowl, or whisk a fresh yolk with a spoonful of water over barely simmering water to a light ribbon
Whisk the broken sauce into it a few drops at a time
Once it takes and thickens, whisk in the rest in a thin stream
Check it coats a spoon and holds a line drawn through it, loosening it with warm water if needed
Hold it warm in a bain-marie, away from direct heat
steps.distractor: Turn up the heat and whisk hard until the sauce pulls back together
steps.why: The heat comes off first and the chef hears straight away. A greasy split comes back when it is rebuilt a droplet at a time on a fresh base, but a truly scrambled sauce does not: heat has cooked the yolk. Only once it takes does the stream speed up.

matches.title: Butter from melted to black
matches.prompt: Match each stage of butter in a hot pan, from melted to black, to what the cook sees and smells.
pairs: A quiet, pale yellow liquid with no browning yet
Loud crackling and a white foam as the water boils off
The crackling quietens and the first brown flecks appear
Hazelnut-brown specks and a smell of toasted nuts: stop it now
A deep, dark brown, past hazelnut but not yet black: the moment for vinegar and capers
Black specks and a bitter, smoky smell: pour it away

matches.prompt: Match each broken or failing emulsion to the rescue a cook reaches for.
pairs: Mayonnaise split into a thin, oily pool
Whisk it drop by drop into a fresh yolk in a clean bowl
Beurre blanc starting to oil out from heat
Off the heat, whisk in a cube or two of cold butter
Whisk it slowly into a spoonful of warm reduction or cream
Butter sauce set thick and dull from cold
Warm it very gently while whisking, never with a blast of heat
Sauce turned stiff and glassy, with a sheen of fat at the edge
Whisk in a spoonful of warm water at once
Whisk in a spoonful of cold water off the heat, then strain out the grains
Hollandaise scrambled into curds of cooked egg
Nothing brings it back: start a new batch
